description: We’re Pixel Pilgrims, a team driven by curiosity, innovation and a passion for exploring new possibilities through technology. With TECTRA, we’re combining satellite radar, GPS data and AI to study subtle ground movements along the Kopili Fault in Northeast India. We’re doing this to better understand how our planet changes beneath the surface. Our aim is to make complex space-based data easier to understand and contribute to the future of earthquake research.
summary:
TECTRA (Tectonic Temporal Risk Analysis) is an autonomous, real-time seismic hazard observatory developed for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Challenge, "Dancing with the SARs." Focused on the active Kopili Fault Corridor along the Assam–Meghalaya tectonic boundary in Northeast India, TECTRA transforms multi-frequency Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite data and continuous ground GPS telemetry into clear, actionable crustal strain intelligence.

To solve the challenge of dense tropical jungle canopies and heavy monsoon weather that blind standard single-band radar, TECTRA fuses canopy-penetrating NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band (24.0 cm) observations with European Sentinel-1 C-band (5.55 cm) radar and a 16-station regional GNSS network. A chained four-model AI consensus architecture—combining multi-pass temporal memory with a Bayesian decision meta-learner—automatically filters out static mountain moisture delays while validating genuine subsurface fault slip, streaming live diagnostics to an interactive 3D web observatory.

By bridging complex orbital radar archives with accessible, false-alarm-resistant risk visualization, TECTRA prevents public panic and helps protect millions living along vulnerable tectonic fault zones.
details:
TECTRA (Tectonic Temporal Risk Analysis) is an autonomous, real-time planetary geodetic observatory and seismic hazard monitoring platform built by Team Pixel Pilgrims for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Challenge ("Dancing with the SARs").
Focused on the Kopili Fault Corridor (25.75°N, 92.25°E) along the Assam–Meghalaya tectonic boundary in Northeast India, TECTRA fuses multi-frequency Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite imagery with continuous ground-based GPS telemetry to detect genuine pre-seismic crustal strain while filtering out weather and terrain false alarms.

The platform operates through a three-stage end-to-end pipeline:

  1. Autonomous Satellite Ingestion & Radar Signal Processing: A scheduled cloud orchestrator authenticates with NASA Earthdata (earthaccess) to stream multi-frequency radar granules—NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band (24.0 cm) and ESA Sentinel-1 C-band (5.55 cm)—alongside a 16-station regional GNSS/GPS network.
    • Deep-Ground Radar Specialist (NISAR L-Band CNN-GNN): Penetrates dense tropical forest canopy to extract 5D dislocation physics latents, epistemic uncertainty, hazard probability, and estimated Time-to-Failure (TTF).
    • Surface Radar & GPS Specialist (Sentinel-1 C-Band CNN-GNN): Cross-examines surface coherence against a localized 16-node radial-basis GNSS network.
    • Multi-Temporal Sequence Memory (Bidirectional GRU Head): Evaluates 3-pass sequential radar histories to distinguish stationary mountain moisture from progressive pre-seismic fault creep acceleration.
    • Bayesian Consensus Meta-Learner: Ingests logits, epistemic uncertainties, resolved fault slip, and topographic scarp delay to dynamically assign sensor trust weights and execute automated false-alarm vetoes.
  2. Interactive 3D Geodetic Observatory (tectra-observatory.vercel.app): Normalized telemetry payloads and Base64 InSAR displacement heatmaps are pushed via authenticated webhooks to Upstash Redis and rendered inside a real-time web workbench featuring a 3D WebGL Earth globe, a draggable Optical-vs-NISAR split-screen radar viewport, a continental plate-velocity tracker (~40 mm/yr northeast convergence), and a 0–20 km subsurface crustal depth slicer.

Key Benefits

  • Automated False-Alarm Immunity: In our live November 15, 2026 production run, a steep 45.32 mm topographic moisture delay along the Meghalaya escarpment caused single-pass L-band radar to spike to 98.3% (CRITICAL). TECTRA’s 3-pass temporal memory enabled the Bayesian meta-learner to cut single-pass L-band trust to 0% and hold the final assessment at 3.45% (NORMAL).
  • All-Weather, Through-Canopy Visibility: Long-wavelength L-band radar (24.0 cm) pierces Northeast India’s dense jungle foliage where shorter C-band waves (5.55 cm) scatter off treetops.
  • Accessible Risk Communication: Translates complex interferometric radar phases into plain-English status indicators, visual comparison sliders, and transparent AI attribution shares.

Intended Impact

Northeast India lies within Seismic Zone V, where millions of residents live along active intracontinental structures such as the Kopili Fault and Main Himalayan Frontal Thrust. TECTRA bridges the gap between petabyte-scale orbital radar missions like NISAR and practical civil preparedness—empowering disaster-response officials, geoscientists, and local communities with early-stage crustal strain intelligence while preventing false-alarm panic and alert fatigue.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3.
  • AI & Radar Processing: PyTorch, ONNX, ONNX Runtime, earthaccess, h5py, tifffile, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib.
  • Web & 3D Geospatial Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Three.js / WebGL, MapLibre GL, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 Canvas (in-browser Okada dislocation modeling).
  • Cloud & DevOps Infrastructure: Kaggle Notebooks (headless automated orchestrator), Upstash Redis (Mumbai bom1 serverless KV store), Vercel (tectra-observatory.vercel.app), GitHub, Telegram Bot API.
  • Hardware: Cloud NVIDIA T4 GPUs (via Google Colab and Kaggle) used for training all four PyTorch models, compiling ONNX binaries, and running automated multi-gigabyte satellite ingestion pipelines, paired with a local ASUS ROG Strix G16 workstation (AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX CPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 GPU with CUDA acceleration in an Ubuntu WSL2 + Windows dual environment) for signal-processing tests and full-stack web observatory development.

How Our Project Is Creative

TECTRA is the first autonomous, dual-band orbital seismic observatory—fusing NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band and European Sentinel-1 radar with a self-auditing 4-AI consensus engines to detect underground fault stress while eliminating monsoon false alarms.

  • AI "Referee" Consensus Gating: Rather than hiding predictions behind a single black-box model, TECTRA orchestrates an explicit cross-examination between independent L-band, C-band, and temporal-memory models governed by a Bayesian meta-learner whose live trust percentages are displayed openly to the user.
  • Historical 2021 Assam M6.0 Physics Reconstruction: Because NISAR had not yet launched during the April 2021 Assam earthquake, we paired actual 2021 Sentinel-1 radar scans (which scattered off forest canopies at 14.2%) with physics-simulated NISAR L-band interferograms reconstructed from the historical ground shift (isolating 18.40 mm of deep slip at 84.1%) to validate a 78.4% (CRITICAL) consensus warning (~4.2-day window).
  • Dual-Spectrum "X-Ray" Viewport & AI Persona Auditing: Combines an interactive optical-to-radar split slider with automated multi-persona AI simulations that audited the observatory’s clarity and trustworthiness through the perspectives of a skeptical geophysicist, a disaster-response official, and an everyday citizen.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Regional Geography & Monsoon Climate: Designed specifically around Assam–Meghalaya’s dense vegetation cover, heavy monsoon water vapor, and steep escarpment elevation gradients that routinely degrade single-frequency interferometry.
  • Operational Resilience & Fault Tolerance: Implemented isolated scratch caches, 4 MB chunked HTTP streaming, BigTIFF memory mapping, and timeout fallback logic so multi-gigabyte satellite downloads or temporary sensor dropouts never crash the runner or trigger false critical alerts.
  • Human Psychology & Ergonomics: Adopted a calm, scientific observatory aesthetic (inspired by NASA JPL Eyes and ESA Copernicus) with plain-language explanations and a desktop-first viewport policy (>= 1024px) so dense geodetic charts and fault maps are never compressed or misread on small mobile screens.
